newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian "misfit" killer deserves pity, says judge.
newsitem.headline: Australian "misfit" killer deserves pity, says judge.

text.p: Modern Australia's worst mass murderer, Martin Bryant, is a grossly disturbed man who in the eyes of the law deserves pity as well as condemnation for his chilling massacre of 35 people at Port Arthur in April.

In sentencing Bryant, 29, to jail on Friday for "the term of his natural life", Judge William Cox said the blond youth, sitting relaxed and almost carefree in the dock of the Tasmanian Supreme Court, was a pathetic misfit of little intelligence.
"He clearly has a mental condition which rendered him less capable than those of normal healthy mind of appreciating the enormity of his conduct or its effect upon others," Cox said.
"That the prisoner, through these handicaps...has developed into a pathetic social misfit calls for understanding and pity, even though his actions demand condemnation," he said.
Prosecutor Damian Bugg agreed, saying the case was sad.
"I feel, I must say, fairly sad about it all. He is a fairly pathetic social misfit, isn't he? It's pretty tragic really," Bugg told reporters after the sentencing.

Bryant himself, in keeping with what psychiatrists have termed his "inappropriate" behaviour, showed no reaction. In the hearings, he sometimes giggled and took casual sips of water as harrowing details of the massacre were read out to the court.
He confessed to the April 28 murders and 37 other charges, including 20 of attempted murder, two weeks ago after initially denying them all, claiming to police that he had gone surfing.
A childhood bully who liked to torment animals, Bryant grew up friendless in this close-knit island state of Tasmania and as an adult nursed a deep grudge against society, the court heard.

The only son of a dock worker and his wife, Bryant was born on May 7, 1967, and raised in the island's capital, Hobart. An aggressive child prone to violent outbursts, he was a torment to his parents who vainly persisted in seeking treatment for him.
Bryant left school at 15, never took a job, and his first sexual experience was with prostitutes.
In recent years, the loner travelled the world in search of a friend, using money bequeathed to him by an elderly woman who in his early 20s had been his only companion.

The eccentric middle-aged Helen Harvey had employed Bryant to perform chores for her in the late 1980s and took him in as a live-in companion in 1990. An heir to a fortune, she died in a car crash in 1992 and left her estate to Bryant.
Bryant's father, Maurice, the only other supportive or controlling influence in Bryant's life, drowned himself on a farm dam near Port Arthur in August 1993, the court heard.
Bryant soon took to jet-setting, taking numerous overseas trips within a matter of weeks "to meet up with normal people" in city cafes in Asia, Europe and the United States.
He tried to strike up conversations with strangers but became enraged when they shunned him, Bryant's lawyer, John Avery, told the court, quoting from a psychiatric report.

In two years, Bryant took about 10 trips abroad and visited Singapore, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Tokyo, Auckland, Los Angeles, Miami, London, Frankfurt, Vienna, Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Sweden and Poland. Each time he returned to Australia disappointed.
"He became increasingly unhappy and angry at not having any friends," the report said. About a year ago he decided he had "had enough", it quoted Bryant as saying.

He contemplated suicide, but a plan formed in his mind in early 1996 of a murderous rampage among the ruins of Port Arthur, a convict settlement where some of Australia's most brutal colonial history was written.
Bryant took a girlfriend in the months before the massacre, but his mind was made up. He refuses to explain why he went ahead with his deadly shooting spree.
Asked why he chose Port Arthur, Bryant replied: "A lot of violence has happened there. It must be the most violent place in Australia. It seemed the right place."
Psychiatrist Ian Sale, hired by the prosecution, believes Bryant suffers from a rare, untreatable personality disorder, Asperger's Syndrome, which is similar in some ways to autism.
"Perhaps people should see him as some freak of nature, some natural disaster, rather than some malicious human being."
